_comment: Public footage bundles. Every machine downloads the same bytes from a permanent URL and
checks the sha256 before using them, so a run on real footage is reproducible without
anybody having to ship a video file — which is what the generated fixture existed to work
around, and what a personal recording could never offer.
Why Wikimedia: upload.wikimedia.org URLs are permanent and content-addressed by path, the
licence of every file is machine-readable, and nothing behind them expires or rotates.
Stock libraries were rejected: Pexels and Pixabay read as CC0 but forbid redistributing
content 'on a Standalone basis', and their URLs are not stable.
Codec note: the LGPL ffmpeg this benchmark prefers has no software AV1 decoder — its only
av1 entry is hardware-only, and fails on hardware without an AV1 block. Several otherwise
ideal Commons screencasts are AV1 and therefore unusable. Sources here are VP8/VP9.

wikipedia-browse.description: A Wikipedia article browsed in a desktop browser, with a talking-head camera track — the shape of a real product demo.
notes: Neither clip carries cursor telemetry — a downloaded video never does. The pointer track is generated from the fixture seed, so it is identical on every machine but does not follow the cursor visible in the footage.

Both clips are 25 fps at the source and are conformed to the 60 fps target during preparation, before any measurement starts. Left at 25, every app would have to convert the rate mid-export — duplicating frames is nearly free, interpolating motion is not — and the ratio would partly measure conversion strategy rather than compositing. The screen clip is also trimmed to the first 60 s.

Conforming 25 to 60 duplicates frames rather than inventing them: 35 of every 60 frames repeat, which compresses more cheaply than a native 60 fps capture would. Every app and the floor receive the identical file, so ratios hold, but absolute seconds from this bundle run lower than from native 60 fps footage.
